messages.content:
You are a clinical validator checking whether a PTSD case
vignette accurately reflects a patient's required cognitive connections.

You will receive:
- A vignette to validate
- A list of REQUIRED edges that must appear
- A list of ACTIVE components that must appear

---

COMPONENT SYNONYMS
Each component may appear by its exact name or any accepted synonym:
  Triggers            → "triggers", "reminders", "cues", "triggering stimuli"
  Negative Appraisals → "negative appraisals", "negative beliefs", "appraisals", "distorted beliefs"
  Memory              → "intrusive memory", "trauma memory", "traumatic memory", "the memory"
  Threat              → "sense of threat", "perceived threat", "threat", "feeling of danger"
  Maladaptive Strategies → "maladaptive strategies", "avoidance", "maladaptive coping", "safety behaviours"

---

CAUSAL STANDARD
A required edge A→B is SATISFIED if, within the same paragraph:
  - Both A and B (or their synonyms) appear, AND
  - The paragraph conveys — through any language — that A influences, drives, or leads to B.
This includes direct causal sentences, sequential structure, or connecting phrases
like "because of", "this meant", "so", "which led", "as a result", "consequently", "in turn".
A required edge is MISSING only if no paragraph conveys the A→B relationship at all.

---

SECTION 1 — COMPONENT CHECK
Active components (must appear in the vignette):
  - Memory
  - Negative Appraisals
  - Triggers

Confirm each component appears as a described feature of the patient's presentation.
This is an internal check only — do NOT add component results to violations.

---

SECTION 2 — REQUIRED EDGES
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Memory
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Memory → Negative Appraisals
  - Memory → Triggers

For each edge, apply the causal standard above.
- If satisfied: do nothing — only failures are reported.
- If missing: add it to violations and explain in one sentence what causal relationship is absent.

Validate the following vignette against the cognitive graph.

Arjun is a 26-year-old editor for a local news website, living in a midwestern city with his wife, Priya. Eight months ago, driving home from a late shift, he was pulled over by two officers. One, a tall woman, ordered him out of the car, then forced him face-down on the hot asphalt while the other searched his vehicle. The summer pavement burned against his cheek and palms, and he smelled the mix of gasoline and her floral perfume. He was released after twenty minutes—a case of mistaken plates—but the memory lodged itself like a splinter. Now, when he thinks back, the olfactory surge returns unexpectedly: that same floral-gasoline mix, and with it a wave of grief so dense he has to sit down. Sometimes his whole body goes rigid, arms pinned underneath him as if he is still lying there, and he feels the heat radiating from the floor. The most frightening moments come when Priya touches his arm or brushes past him—the sensation of a woman’s presence, alone, triggers a sudden dissociative feeling, as if the room becomes a stage and he is watching himself from somewhere unreachable.

In the weeks that followed, Arjun began to avoid anything that might bring back the asphalt heat. He stopped wearing fitted collared shirts because the pressure on his chest reminded him of the handcuffs. At the office, he requested to work from home three days a week, citing a need for quiet focus. But the real problem, he told himself, was that he couldn’t trust his own reactions. *I should have been able to shake this off*, he thought. *Other people go through worse and they don't fall apart*. He came to see himself as a lousy coper, someone fundamentally weak. That appraisal hollowed out the rest of his life: nothing felt meaningful anymore—his editing work, once satisfying, now seemed pointless; he stopped replying to friends because nothing good could happen to him anyway. The more he believed that, the more he dreaded encountering a trigger. A warm breeze on a spring afternoon—temperature on his skin—would make him think, *Here we go again, I can't even handle the weather*, and that thought would flood him with the smell and the grief and the frozen posture all over again. Each intrusion confirmed his failure, and each failure sharpened his vigilance for the next trigger.

His occupational environment became an unavoidable proving ground. As an editor, he frequently needed to meet with reporters one-on-one to review copy. He began declining in-person meetings with female colleagues, pushing them to email or Slack instead, inventing reasons about deadlines. When a female junior reporter knocked on his office door, his stomach dropped; he kept his eyes on the screen, his voice clipped, and let her leave as quickly as possible. He knew this was odd, but the alternative—being alone with a woman in that small room—felt like stepping back onto the hot asphalt. The dissociative feeling would creep in before he could stop it: a vertigo of unreality, his hands going numb, the walls seeming to slide sideways. His manager noticed the shift and pulled him aside, asking if everything was okay. Arjun muttered about stress, but the conversation only deepened his conviction that he was failing at work, at marriage, at everything.

At home, Priya grew worried. He had become distant, quick to irritability, and he flinched when she touched him unexpectedly. She pressed him to talk, but Arjun felt he had no language for what was happening—only the raw grief that surfaced when he remembered the officer’s perfume, the heat, the complete helplessness. The more he tried to push the memory away, the more vividly it returned, and each return fed his belief that his future held nothing but this cycle. What finally drove him to seek help was a night when Priya sat down beside him on the couch and quietly said, “I don’t know how to reach you anymore.” He looked at her face and realized he had been treating her presence as a threat. That recognition—that he had lost the ability to be close to the person he loved most—cracked something open. He is still afraid: afraid that talking about it will make the smell come back permanently, afraid that a therapist will confirm he really is a bad coper. But the prospect of losing Priya is worse, and so he arrives with a tight jaw and a hope he barely dares to name—that somewhere inside all this numbness, meaning might still be recoverable.

violation_explanations: The vignette does not convey that negative appraisals cause or influence triggers; it only shows triggers causing negative appraisals.
